name: Battles of Khalkhin Gol
info: Soviet and Mongolian forces under Georgy Zhukov fought Japanese and Manchukoan forces on the disputed Mongolia-Manchukuo border in 1939, and by 31 August had trapped and destroyed the Japanese forces on the Mongolian side.

facts.date: 11 May to 15 September 1939; the cease-fire agreed on 15 September took effect at 1:10 pm on 16 September. The main Soviet offensive began on 20 August
facts.place: Along the river Khalkhin Gol near Nomonhan, on the disputed border between the Mongolian People's Republic and Manchukuo, in present-day Mongolia and China
facts.sides: The Soviet Union and Mongolia under Georgy Zhukov, with about 50,000 Soviet and Mongolian soldiers in the attack on the east bank on 20 August; Japan and Manchukuo, with the Kwantung Army's 23rd Infantry Division under Lieutenant General Michitarō Komatsubara at the point of contact
facts.outcome: Soviet victory: the Japanese forces on the Mongolian side of the border were destroyed by 31 August, and a cease-fire followed on 15 September.

t: The two sides disagreed about where the border lay: the Japanese held that it was the Khalkhin Gol, the Mongolians and Soviets that it ran 16 kilometres to the east, just east of Nomonhan.
Zhukov's offensive of 20 August pinned the Japanese in the centre and swept armoured units round both flanks, trapping the Japanese 23rd Infantry Division when the wings linked up on 25 August.
Japanese casualty figures range from about 19,714 in the Sixth Army's medical data to 35,000 to 36,000 reported by a minister, and the Soviet claims for them rose from 29,085 to 61,000.
dyk: The Japanese record the fighting as the Nomonhan Incident, after Nomonhan Burd Obo, yet it involved aircraft, tanks and tens of thousands of troops, and it ended only with a cease-fire.
ev: The Soviet Union and Mongolia sign a Mutual Assistance Pact, allowing Soviet troops into Mongolia
A Mongolian cavalry unit is driven back across the Khalkhin Gol by Manchukoan cavalry
Soviet and Mongolian forces surround and destroy the Azuma force
The Japanese attack in two prongs, but both are thrown back by 9 July
A second large Japanese assault on the Kawatama Bridge is called off on 25 July
Zhukov opens his offensive with artillery and 557 aircraft
The Soviet wings link up near Nomonhan and trap the Japanese 23rd Infantry Division
The Soviet Union and Japan agree a cease-fire

sections.background:
After the Japanese occupation of Manchuria in 1931, Japan turned its military interests to the Soviet territories that bordered the area. The Soviet Union and the People's Republic of Mongolia signed a Mutual Assistance Pact in March 1936, allowing Soviet troops into Mongolia, and in the same year Japan signed the Anti-Comintern Pact. After Japan's full invasion of China in July 1937, the Soviet Union sent the 57th Special Corps under Ivan Konev to Mongolia. Genrikh Lyushkov, a Soviet NKVD major general, defected to Japan for fear of the Great Purge, taking secret documents that allegedly revealed the dire situation of the Soviet army in the Far East. The first major Soviet-Japanese border incident, the Battle of Lake Khasan, came in 1938 in Primorye.

In 1939 Manchuria was a puppet state of Japan known as Manchukuo, and Mongolia a communist state allied with the Soviet Union. The Japanese maintained that the border between them was the Khalkhin Gol, which flows into Lake Buir. The Mongolians and their Soviet allies maintained that it ran 16 kilometres east of the river, just east of Nomonhan. The principal occupying army of Manchukuo, Japan's Kwantung Army, had instructions from the Japanese Cabinet to strengthen and fortify Manchukuo's borders. Stationed in Manchuria for a long time, it had become largely autonomous and tended to act without approval from the Japanese government, or even against its direction.
sections.forces:
The fighting began on 11 May 1939, when a Mongolian cavalry unit of 70 to 90 men entered the disputed area in search of grazing and Manchu cavalry drove it back across the river. Both sides then increased their forces. On 5 June Zhukov, the new corps commander, arrived with more motorized and armoured forces, accompanied by the air commander Yakov Smushkevich; Zhamyangiyn Lhagvasuren of the Mongolian army became his deputy. Zhukov's army was 748 kilometres from its base of supply and he assembled 2,600 trucks to feed it. In early July the Japanese had only 600 trucks, rising to 1,000 by the end of the month, of which only 75% were operable.

For their assault in July the Japanese used three regiments and part of a fourth under Colonel Shinichiro Sumi, to cross the river and take Baintsagan Hill, and the 1st Tank Corps under Lieutenant General Yasuoka Masaomi, made up of the 3rd and 4th Tank Regiments with infantry, engineers and artillery, to attack the east bank.

By 20 August Zhukov, using at least 4,000 trucks from the base at Chita, 600 kilometres away, had three rifle divisions, two tank divisions and two more tank brigades (around 498 BT-5 and BT-7 tanks), two motorized infantry divisions and over 550 fighters and bombers. The Mongolians committed two cavalry divisions. At the point of contact the Kwantung Army had only the 23rd Infantry Division, equal with its attached forces to two light infantry divisions, with its headquarters at Hailar, over 150 kilometres from the fighting. Japanese intelligence tracked the build-up but did not provoke an appropriate response from below.
sections.course:
On 14 May Lieutenant Colonel Yaozo Azuma led the reconnaissance regiment of the 23rd Infantry Division into the area and the Mongolians withdrew, but when they and the Soviets returned and Azuma's force moved to evict them, they surrounded it on 28 May and destroyed it. It lost eight officers and 97 men killed and one officer and 33 men wounded, 63% total casualties. On 27 June the Japanese Army Air Force's 2nd Air Brigade struck the Soviet airbase at Tamsak-Bulak. The strike, ordered by the Kwantung Army without permission from army headquarters in Tokyo, succeeded, but Tokyo then forbade any more.

The July assault began with the northern force crossing the Khalkhin Gol and taking Baintsagan Hill. Zhukov counterattacked with 450 tanks and armoured cars, which, though unsupported by infantry, attacked on three sides and nearly encircled the Japanese, who had only one pontoon bridge for supplies and recrossed the river on 5 July. The Yasuoka Detachment attacked on the night of 2 July, lost over half its armour without breaking through, was thrown back on 9 July, and was dissolved. A second assault on 23 July, backed by an artillery barrage that used more than half the ammunition stores, failed and was abandoned on 25 July.

At 05:45 on 20 August Soviet artillery and 557 aircraft struck the Japanese, and about 50,000 Soviet and Mongolian soldiers attacked the east bank. With the Japanese pinned down by the centre, armoured units swept round the flanks and attacked from the rear in a classic double envelopment. The wings linked up at Nomonhan on 25 August, trapping the 23rd Division. A Japanese counterattack on 26 August failed, as did a breakout on 27 August, and by 31 August the Japanese forces on the Mongolian side were destroyed.
sections.aftermath:
The Soviet Union and Japan agreed to a cease-fire on 15 September, which took effect at 1:10 pm the next day. Japanese military records reported approximately 20,000 battle and non-battle casualties, 162 aircraft lost in combat and 42 tanks disabled, of which 29 were repaired. Roughly 500 to 600 Japanese and Manchus were taken prisoner; because military doctrine prohibited surrender, most were listed as killed in action for the benefit of their families.

Zhukov reported Soviet casualties in the offensive from 20 August as 9,284, among them 1,701 dead and missing and 7,583 wounded. For the whole campaign Soviet equipment losses were 253 tanks, 250 aircraft, 96 artillery pieces and 133 armoured cars. Mongolian casualties were 556 to 990, including 280 killed and 710 wounded.

Zhukov won the first of his four Hero of the Soviet Union awards, as did Grigori Shtern and Yakov Smushkevich, who were both executed in the 1941 purges. Zhukov was promoted and moved west to the Kiev district. The Kwantung Army earned the displeasure of officials in Tokyo, less for its defeat than because it had started and escalated the fighting without government authorization. The Soviet Union and Japan signed the Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact in April 1941.
sections.sources:
The casualty figures are the most disputed part of the record. Japanese military records give about 20,000 casualties. The Sixth Army's medical data give 7,696 killed, 8,647 wounded, 1,021 missing and 2,350 sick, a total of 19,714, while Kwantung Army headquarters gave 8,629 killed and 9,087 injured, excluding sick. In November 1939 the American consulate in Harbin claimed to hold authoritative information that casualties reached 30,000, and in October the Agricultural Minister Yukio Sakurauchi reported 35,000 to 36,000 out of 40,000 participants. A monument of September 1942 attributed 9,471 Japanese and 202 Manchus to the campaign.

The Soviets first claimed to have inflicted 29,085 casualties, then 52,000 to 55,000, then 61,000 in their official histories. For their own losses, Grigoriy Krivosheev cited 7,974 killed and 15,251 wounded in 1993, and in 2001 gave revised figures of 9,703 dead and missing, 15,251 wounded and 701 sick, a total of 25,655. Boris Sokolov cites a higher number of sick, 2,225, writing that the lower figure reflects only patients treated in the Trans-Baikal Military District.
sections.legacy:
The victory is credited with altering the course of the Second World War. Together with Chinese resistance and the German-Soviet non-aggression pact, which removed the basis of the army's policy against the Soviet Union, the defeat moved the Imperial General Staff away from the north-strike policy favoured by the Army, which wanted Siberia as far as Lake Baikal for its resources. Support shifted to the south-strike policy favoured by the Navy, aimed at Southeast Asia and the Dutch East Indies. Masanobu Tsuji, who had helped instigate the incident, later wrote that Soviet firepower at Nomonhan convinced him not to attack the Soviet Union in 1941. On 24 June 1941 Japan's leaders resolved not to intervene in the German-Soviet war for the time being, and Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December.

Zhukov used the experience at Moscow in December 1941, and at Stalingrad in Operation Uranus a year later, using a technique very similar to Khalkhin Gol. The Japanese increased tank production from 500 annually to 1,200 in 1939 and introduced the Type 1 47 mm anti-tank gun. After the war the Soviet Union charged fourteen Japanese at the Tokyo tribunal over the fighting, and Kenji Doihara, Hiranuma Kiichirō and Seishirō Itagaki were convicted on these charges. The Mongolian town of Choibalsan and Ulaanbaatar have museums to Zhukov and the battle, and the anniversaries have been marked with the presidents of Russia and Mongolia.

summary: In 1939 Soviet and Mongolian forces under Zhukov fought Japanese and Manchukoan forces over the Mongolia-Manchukuo border. His offensive of 20 August trapped the Japanese 23rd Division, and a cease-fire followed on 15 September. Japan afterwards turned its strategy south.
references: Alvin D. Coox, Nomonhan: Japan Against Russia, 1939 (Stanford University Press, 1985)
Stuart D. Goldman, Nomonhan, 1939; The Red Army's Victory That Shaped World War II (Naval Institute Press, 2012)
Dimitar Nedialkov, In The Skies of Nomonhan, Japan vs Russia, May–September 1939 (Crecy Publishing, 2011)
Vladimir R. Kotelnikov, Air War Over Khalkhin Gol, The Nomonhan Incident (SAM publications, 2010)
notes: Left out: Lyushkov's defection date, given only as '13 June' with no year, so I gave no date; the Lyushkov documents are 'allegedly' revealing, as the article says.
The article says 'Soviet–Japanese Neutrality Pact' was signed in April 1941 and that the two reaffirmed neutrality in August 1941; I gave April only.

The Japanese casualty table (IJA battle casualties for selected periods) and the aircraft strength tables are empty in the saved text, so no figures from them are used; the aircraft loss summary is left out for length.

Disputed or self-contradictory: Japanese casualty totals (19,714 medical data; 8,629 killed plus 9,087 injured in headquarters records; 30,000; 35-36,000 of 40,000); the 1942 monument gives 9,471 Japanese and 202 Manchus; Soviet claims 29,085 to 61,000; Krivosheev's 1993 and 2001 totals; Sokolov on sick. The July 1939 order-of-battle tank list is not used.
Truck numbers: 2,600 (July) versus at least 4,000 (August) for Zhukov, both given; the article says the Soviet army was 748 km from base in July but the Chita base 600 km in August.
The article says the 3 August and 7-8 August Soviet probing attacks were thrown back with about 1,000 Soviet dead against 85 Japanese casualties; left out for length.
The article says the Soviet armoured counterattack in July had 450 tanks and armoured cars and was unsupported by infantry; 'nearly encircled' kept.

'Nomonhan was the first use of airpower on a massive scale' and 'first fighter-bomber offensive in Soviet Air Force history' and 'the decisive engagements' are the article's own claims; I did not repeat them as fact.
